claim: Hair follicles are highly conserved touch sensory organs in the hairy skin that covers most of the mammalian body surface and detects touch signals essential for development and survival.
source: Hair follicles are highly conserved touch sensory organs in the hairy skin that covers most of the mammalian body surface and detects touch signals essential for development and survival (Lumpkin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lumpkin et al., 2010

claim: Hair follicles are innervated by mechanosensory end organs called lanceolate complexes, which are composed of parallel, longitudinally aligned low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR) axonal endings and terminal Schwann cell processes.
source: Hair follicles are innervated by mechanosensory end organs called lanceolate complexes, which are composed of parallel, longitudinally aligned low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR) axonal endings and terminal Schwann cell processes (Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zimmerman et al., 2014

claim: Hair follicles are connected to arrector pili muscles (APMs), forming a unique regenerating motile sensory organ.
source: Hair follicles are also connected to arrector pili muscles (APMs), thus forming a unique regenerating motile sensory organ.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about hair follicle anatomy

claim: The bulge is the permanent portion of the hair follicle where epidermal stem cells reside.
source: These two hair follicle appendages attach to the permanent portion of the hair follicle, known as the bulge, where epidermal stem cells reside.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about hair follicle anatomy

claim: Hair follicle epidermal stem cells are heterogeneous in their molecular and functional properties and compartmentalized along the longitudinal axis of the hair follicle.
source: Hair follicle epidermal stem cells are heterogeneous in their molecular and functional properties and compartmentalized along the longitudinal axis of the hair follicle (Figure 1A) (Solanas and Benitah, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Solanas and Benitah, 2013 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The mid-bulge region contains CD34+ slow-cycling epidermal stem cells that serve as a reservoir of epidermal stem cells.
source: The mid-bulge region contains CD34+ slow-cycling epidermal stem cells that serve as a reservoir of epidermal stem cells and were once thought to be the master stem cells at the top of the epidermal hierarchy.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about mid-bulge stem cells

claim: The upper-bulge is a niche for Gli1+ epidermal stem cells that contribute to hair follicle regeneration and wound healing of interfollicular epidermis.
source: For example, the upper-bulge is a niche for Gli1+epidermal stem cells and they contribute to hair follicle regeneration and wound healing of interfollicular epidermis (Brownell et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brownell et al., 2011

claim: Mid-bulge epidermal stem cells create a specialized basement membrane containing nephronectin, providing a niche for APM development and anchorage.
source: Consistent with this idea, it has been reported that mid-bulge epidermal stem cells create a specialized basement membrane containing nephronectin, thereby providing a niche for APM development and anchorage (Fujiwara et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujiwara et al., 2011

claim: Follicle epidermis–derived BDNF is critical for follicle-nerve interactions.
source: Follicle epidermis–derived BDNF is also critical for follicle-nerve interactions (Rutlin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rutlin et al., 2014

claim: Neurogenesis-related Gene Ontology (GO) terms are over-represented in Gli1+ bulge epidermal stem cells.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) indicated that neurogenesis-related Gene Ontology (GO) terms are over-represented in Gli1+ bulge epidermal stem cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: Upper-bulge epidermal stem cells express neurotrophic factors including Grp, Bdnf and Nrtn.
source: Prominent gene-annotation clusters in both Group I and Group II cells encode proteins involved in nervous system development, including the neurotrophic factors Grp, Bdnf and Nrtn and the keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness syndrome gene Gjb2 (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1E and F

claim: Multiple ECM genes are upregulated in the upper-bulge compartment, including Aspn, Crispld1, Egfl6, and the deafness-related ECM genes Col4a3 and Col4a4.
source: Multiple ECM genes are also upregulated in the upper-bulge compartment, including Aspn, Crispld1, Egfl6, and the deafness-related ECM genes Col4a3 and Col4a4 (Mochizuki et al., 1994) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1E and F, with citation to Mochizuki et al., 1994 for deafness-related genes

claim: Eight ECM proteins were deposited in the upper-bulge.
source: On examining the tissue localization of 15 upper-bulge ECM proteins, we found that 8 ECM proteins were deposited in the upper-bulge (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A

claim: EGFL6 exhibited the most restricted localization in the upper-bulge of all types of dorsal hair follicles and showed a unique C-shaped pattern with a gap at the rostral side of the hair follicle.
source: Among them, EGFL6 (EGF-like domain multiple 6) exhibited the most restricted localization in the upper-bulge of all types of dorsal hair follicles and showed a unique C-shaped pattern with a gap at the rostral side of the hair follicle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Skin nerve endings terminate at the EGFL6 deposition sites.
source: βIII-tubulin staining showed that skin nerve endings terminate at the EGFL6 deposition sites (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: EGFL6 is closely associated with longitudinal lanceolate parallel LTMR axonal endings of lanceolate complexes.
source: Magnified 3D images revealed the close association of EGFL6 with longitudinal lanceolate parallel LTMR axonal endings of lanceolate complexes, which are activated by tactile stimuli (Figure 2C) (Bai et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Bai et al., 2015

claim: EGFL6 is closely associated with longitudinal processes of nestin-positive non-myelinating terminal Schwann cells of lanceolate complexes.
source: Magnified 3D images revealed the close association of EGFL6 with longitudinal lanceolate parallel LTMR axonal endings of lanceolate complexes, which are activated by tactile stimuli (Figure 2C) (Bai et al., 2015), and longitudinal processes of nestin-positive non-myelinating terminal Schwann cells of lanceolate complexes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D

claim: EGFL6 does not show direct contact with blood vessels.
source: A close anatomical association of follicle EGFL6 with blood vessels has been reported (Xiao et al., 2013), but their direct contact was not observed (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2E, contrasting with citation to Xiao et al., 2013

claim: eGFP protein expression in Egfl6-H2b-Egfp reporter mice was enriched in upper-bulge epidermal stem cells at the caudal side of the hair follicle.
source: eGFP protein expression was enriched in upper-bulge epidermal stem cells at the caudal side of the hair follicle, but was not detected in dermal cells around the upper-bulge or dorsal root ganglia neurons that innervate the upper-bulge (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 2F and G

claim: Egfl6 expression was not detected in dermal cells around the upper-bulge or dorsal root ganglia neurons that innervate the upper-bulge.
source: eGFP protein expression was enriched in upper-bulge epidermal stem cells at the caudal side of the hair follicle, but was not detected in dermal cells around the upper-bulge or dorsal root ganglia neurons that innervate the upper-bulge (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 2F and G

claim: An electron-dense amorphous ECM structure surrounds the lanceolate complexes.
source: We identified an electron-dense amorphous ECM structure surrounding the lanceolate complexes (black arrowheads in Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2H

claim: The collar matrix tightly ensheathes the lanceolate complexes.
source: We named this novel structure the 'collar matrix', as it tightly ensheathes the lanceolate complexes.
evidence: Based on electron microscopy observations described in the manuscript

claim: Terminal Schwann cell processes have two openings, at the follicular basement membrane and at the opposite side of the cell, exposing axonal endings and terminal Schwann cell processes to the hair follicle basement membrane and the collar matrix.
source: Terminal Schwann cell processes have two openings, at the follicular basement membrane and at the opposite side of the cell, thus exposing axonal endings and terminal Schwann cell processes to at least two different ECMs, the hair follicle basement membrane and the collar matrix.
evidence: Based on electron microscopy observations described in the manuscript

claim: EGFL6 is detected exclusively in the collar matrix.
source: Although EGFL6 is expressed by the upper-bulge epidermal stem cells, an immunogold-labeled EGFL6 antibody was detected exclusively in the collar matrix (Figure 2I)
evidence: Supported by immunogold electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Upper-bulge epidermal stem cells secrete EGFL6, which is incorporated in the collar matrix that ensheathes lanceolate complexes.
source: Although EGFL6 is expressed by the upper-bulge epidermal stem cells, an immunogold-labeled EGFL6 antibody was detected exclusively in the collar matrix (Figure 2I), indicating that upper-bulge epidermal stem cells secrete EGFL6, which is incorporated in the collar matrix that ensheathes lanceolate complexes (Figure 2J).
evidence: Inferred from expression and localization data shown in Figures 2I and 2J

claim: One skin fibroblast and two glial cell lines adhered to EGFL6.
source: Among nine cell lines tested, one skin fibroblast and two glial cell lines adhered to EGFL6, whereas other cell types, including keratinocytes, did not (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Keratinocytes did not adhere to EGFL6.
source: Among nine cell lines tested, one skin fibroblast and two glial cell lines adhered to EGFL6, whereas other cell types, including keratinocytes, did not (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Upper-bulge epidermal stem cells are incapable of interacting with EGFL6.
source: Among nine cell lines tested, one skin fibroblast and two glial cell lines adhered to EGFL6, whereas other cell types, including keratinocytes, did not (Figure 3B), suggesting that although EGFL6 is derived from the upper-bulge epidermal stem cells, these stem cells are incapable of interacting with EGFL6.
evidence: Inferred from cell adhesion assay data showing keratinocytes do not adhere to EGFL6

claim: Dermal cell lineages interact and adhere to EGFL6.
source: Among nine cell lines tested, one skin fibroblast and two glial cell lines adhered to EGFL6, whereas other cell types, including keratinocytes, did not (Figure 3B), suggesting that although EGFL6 is derived from the upper-bulge epidermal stem cells, these stem cells are incapable of interacting with EGFL6. Instead dermal cell lineages interact and adhere to EGFL6.
evidence: Inferred from cell adhesion assay data showing fibroblast and glial cells adhere to EGFL6

claim: A point mutation in the Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) integrin recognition sequence of EGFL6 (RGE mutant) significantly reduced its cell adhesive ability.
source: A point mutation in the Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) integrin recognition sequence of EGFL6 (RGE mutant) significantly reduced its cell adhesive ability (Figure 3C) (Oberauer et al., 2010; Osada et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Oberauer et al., 2010 and Osada et al., 2005

claim: α8β1 integrin expression was not detected in lanceolate complexes.
source: Although α8β1 integrin has been reported to mediate cell adhesion to EGFL6 (Osada et al., 2005), its expression was not detected in lanceolate complexes (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Osada et al., 2005

claim: Cell adhesion to EGFL6 was inhibited by the αv integrin antibody, but not by the β1 integrin antibody.
source: Thus we further performed cell adhesion inhibition assays with a panel of antibodies that block integrin function and found that cell adhesion to EGFL6 was inhibited by the αv integrin antibody, but not by the β1 integrin antibody (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion inhibition assay data shown in Figure 3E

claim: αv integrin accumulated in lanceolate complexes and colocalized with EGFL6.
source: Consistent with these results, αv integrin accumulated in lanceolate complexes and colocalized with EGFL6 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Deletion of EGFL6 decreased αv integrin and impaired its accumulation.
source: Deletion of EGFL6 decreased αv integrin and impaired its accumulation (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: Integrin αv was localized to the axonal endings of lanceolate complexes and distributed on their collar matrix side.
source: A detailed examination of integrin localization revealed that integrin αv was localized to the axonal endings of lanceolate complexes and distributed on their collar matrix side (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by detailed immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Integrin β1 was enriched at the interface between hair follicles and lanceolate complex endings, where the basement membrane is located, and was also detected at the outer surface of lanceolate complex endings.
source: On the other hand, integrin β1 was enriched at the interface between hair follicles and lanceolate complex endings, where the basement membrane is located, and was also detected at the outer surface of lanceolate complex endings.
evidence: Supported by detailed immunostaining observations described in the manuscript

claim: Integrin α3 accumulated at the inner and outer surfaces of the axonal endings.
source: Integrin α3 accumulated at the inner and outer surfaces of the axonal endings, whereas integrin α6 was preferentially localized to the inner and outer surfaces of terminal Schwann cell protrusions.
evidence: Supported by detailed immunostaining observations described in the manuscript

claim: Integrin α6 was preferentially localized to the inner and outer surfaces of terminal Schwann cell protrusions.
source: Integrin α3 accumulated at the inner and outer surfaces of the axonal endings, whereas integrin α6 was preferentially localized to the inner and outer surfaces of terminal Schwann cell protrusions.
evidence: Supported by detailed immunostaining observations described in the manuscript

claim: EGFL6 induces cell adhesion via αv integrins that accumulate in the axonal endings of lanceolate complexes in an EGFL6-dependent manner.
source: Together, these results show that EGFL6 induces cell adhesion via αv integrins that accumulate in the axonal endings of lanceolate complexes in an EGFL6-dependent manner.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from cell adhesion assays and immunostaining

claim: Egfl6 knockout mice showed misaligned and overlapping structures of axonal endings and terminal Schwann cell processes in 8-week-old second telogen hair follicles.
source: Egfl6 knockout mice showed misaligned and overlapping structures of axonal endings and terminal Schwann cell processes in 8-week-old second telogen hair follicles (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Quantitative 3D histomorphometric analysis revealed a significant increase in overlapping points of axons and terminal Schwann cell protrusions in Egfl6 knockout mice.
source: Quantitative 3D histomorphometric analysis of LTMRs and terminal Schwann cells revealed a significant increase in overlapping points of axons and terminal Schwann cell protrusions in Egfl6 knockout mice (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: The numbers and lengths of axonal endings were unchanged in Egfl6 knockout mice.
source: The numbers and lengths of axonal endings were unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: In Egfl6 knockout tissue, the length, but not the width, of terminal Schwann cell processes was reduced.
source: In Egfl6 knockout tissue, the length, but not the width, of terminal Schwann cell processes was reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: Ultrastructural analysis identified imperfectly sandwiched lanceolate complexes in Egfl6 knockout mice.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of lanceolate complexes identified imperfectly sandwiched lanceolate complexes in the knockout mice, but we did not detect obvious morphological abnormalities in cell–ECM and cell–cell interaction sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: No obvious morphological abnormalities in cell–ECM and cell–cell interaction sites were detected in Egfl6 knockout mice.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of lanceolate complexes identified imperfectly sandwiched lanceolate complexes in the knockout mice, but we did not detect obvious morphological abnormalities in cell–ECM and cell–cell interaction sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The disorganized lanceolate complex structure already occurred at the first telogen (P19) in Egfl6 knockout mice.
source: We also examined the phenotype at the earlier time point, the first telogen (P19), and found that the disorganized lanceolate complex structure already occurred (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Egfl6 knockout mice did not show defects in the hair cycle.
source: Egfl6 knockout mice did not show defects in the hair cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: EGFL6 is required for proper parallel patterning of lanceolate complexes.
source: We conclude that EGFL6 is required for proper parallel patterning of lanceolate complexes.
evidence: Conclusion based on morphological analysis of Egfl6 knockout mice

claim: The median mechanical response threshold of Aδ-LTMRs measured using von Frey hairs was significantly higher in Egfl6 knockout skin.
source: The median mechanical response threshold of Aδ-LTMRs measured using von Frey hairs was significantly higher in knockout skin (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Egfl6 knockout skin exhibits fewer action potentials than wild-type skin at displacements of >32 μm.
source: Averaged touch response patterns showed that knockout skin exhibits fewer action potentials than wild-type skin at displacements of >32 μm (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 5B and C

claim: The median threshold displacement of Aδ-LTMRs was about three times higher in Egfl6 knockout mice.
source: The median threshold displacement of Aδ-LTMRs was about three times higher in the knockout (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Significantly fewer action potentials were detected during the course of the touch stimulus protocol in Egfl6 knockout skin.
source: Significantly fewer action potentials were detected during the course of the touch stimulus protocol in Egfl6 knockout skin (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4G

claim: EGFL6 plays an important role in the excitation of Aδ-LTMRs.
source: These results indicate that EGFL6 plays an important role in the excitation of Aδ-LTMRs.
evidence: Conclusion based on electrophysiological analysis of Egfl6 knockout mice

claim: At the first telogen (P20), the upper-bulge exhibits a single circular peripheral morphology with one hair shaft.
source: We found that at the first telogen (P20), the upper-bulge exhibits a single circular peripheral morphology with one hair shaft, while at the first anagen (P35), the upper-bulge perimeter doubles due to the formation of a new hair follicle rostral to the existing hair follicle (old bulge) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5A–C

claim: At the first anagen (P35), the upper-bulge perimeter doubles due to the formation of a new hair follicle rostral to the existing hair follicle (old bulge).
source: We found that at the first telogen (P20), the upper-bulge exhibits a single circular peripheral morphology with one hair shaft, while at the first anagen (P35), the upper-bulge perimeter doubles due to the formation of a new hair follicle rostral to the existing hair follicle (old bulge) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5A–C

claim: At the second telogen (P49), the upper-bulge perimeter decreased due to a reduction in the new bulge perimeter.
source: At the second telogen (P49), the upper-bulge perimeter decreased due to a reduction in the new bulge perimeter.
evidence: Supported by observations described in the manuscript

claim: The external configuration of the rostral side of the upper-bulge epidermis changes dynamically during the hair follicle regeneration cycle, while the caudal aspect remains stable.
source: Thus, the external configuration of the rostral side of the upper-bulge epidermis changes dynamically during the hair follicle regeneration cycle, while the caudal aspect remains stable.
evidence: Conclusion based on morphological analysis across hair cycle stages

claim: EGFL6 and terminal Schwann cells in the old bulge maintained regular parallel morphologies throughout the hair cycle.
source: Consistent with these signal intensity data, EGFL6 and terminal Schwann cells in the old bulge maintained regular parallel morphologies throughout the hair cycle, while those in the new bulge exhibited diverse morphologies and wider widths in the first anagen (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: EGFL6 and terminal Schwann cells in the new bulge exhibited diverse morphologies and wider widths in the first anagen.
source: Consistent with these signal intensity data, EGFL6 and terminal Schwann cells in the old bulge maintained regular parallel morphologies throughout the hair cycle, while those in the new bulge exhibited diverse morphologies and wider widths in the first anagen (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The polarized distributions of lanceolate complex components toward the caudal side of the hair follicles are induced as the new bulge structure forms at the rostral side of the hair follicle.
source: Thus, the polarized distributions of lanceolate complex components toward the caudal side of the hair follicles are induced as the new bulge structure forms at the rostral side of the hair follicle.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of lanceolate complex distribution across hair cycle stages

claim: The old bulge stably preserves lanceolate complexes irrespective of the stage of hair regeneration cycle.
source: The caudal side of the hair follicle, where the old bulge is maintained by quiescent epidermal stem cells, does not change in morphology, suggesting that the old bulge stably preserves lanceolate complexes irrespective of the stage of hair regeneration cycle.
evidence: Inferred from morphological stability observations

claim: Club hair plucking induces apoptosis in bulge stem cells within 4.5 hr.
source: It has been reported that hair plucking induces apoptosis in bulge stem cells within 4.5 hr (Chen et al., 2015; Ito et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Ito et al., 2002

claim: Epidermal cells with a bright DAPI signal, an indicator of apoptosis, were observed in the old bulge, but not in the new bulge, within 4 hr after club hair plucking.
source: Consistent with this, epidermal cells with a bright DAPI signal, an indicator of apoptosis, were observed in the old bulge, but not in the new bulge, within 4 hr after club hair plucking (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Three days after club hair plucking, the old bulges regressed with a slight decrease in overall follicle perimeter.
source: Three days after plucking, the old bulges regressed with a slight decrease in overall follicle perimeter (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: The club hair plucking procedure specifically depleted the old bulge epidermal cells through inducing apoptosis and changed the topology of the old bulge.
source: Three days after plucking, the old bulges regressed with a slight decrease in overall follicle perimeter (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), but the new follicles remained, suggesting that the club hair plucking procedure specifically depleted the old bulge epidermal cells through inducing apoptosis and changed the topology of the old bulge.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on old vs. new bulge after plucking

claim: In plucked hair follicles, axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes disappeared from the caudal side of the upper-bulge.
source: In these plucked hair follicles, axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes disappeared from the caudal side of the upper-bulge, while ectopic axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes appeared at the rostral side of the upper-bulge (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: In plucked hair follicles, ectopic axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes appeared at the rostral side of the upper-bulge.
source: In these plucked hair follicles, axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes disappeared from the caudal side of the upper-bulge, while ectopic axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes appeared at the rostral side of the upper-bulge (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: The maintenance of the old bulge appears to be critical for sustaining caudally polarized lanceolate complex structure.
source: Thus, the maintenance of the old bulge appears to be critical for sustaining caudally polarized lanceolate complex structure.
evidence: Conclusion based on club hair plucking experiments

claim: EGFL6 remained at the caudal side of the plucked hair follicles even without axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes.
source: This notion is supported by the fact that EGFL6 remained at the caudal side of the plucked hair follicles even without axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes, while the deposition level of EGFL6 was still low at the rostral side (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: The deposition level of EGFL6 was still low at the rostral side of plucked hair follicles.
source: This notion is supported by the fact that EGFL6 remained at the caudal side of the plucked hair follicles even without axon endings and terminal Schwann cell processes, while the deposition level of EGFL6 was still low at the rostral side (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: Lanceolate complex processes in the old bulge retracted after club hair plucking, but EGFL6 matrix remained in the caudal side.
source: This observation suggests that i) lanceolate complex processes in the old bulge retracted after club hair plucking, but EGFL6 matrix remained in the caudal side, and ii) ectopic lanceolate complex processes were formed at the rostral side, but EGFL6 deposition required additional time as observed in lanceolate complex morphogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from EGFL6 distribution patterns after plucking

claim: Ectopic lanceolate complex processes were formed at the rostral side after plucking, but EGFL6 deposition required additional time.
source: This observation suggests that i) lanceolate complex processes in the old bulge retracted after club hair plucking, but EGFL6 matrix remained in the caudal side, and ii) ectopic lanceolate complex processes were formed at the rostral side, but EGFL6 deposition required additional time as observed in lanceolate complex morphogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from EGFL6 distribution patterns after plucking

claim: The formation and preservation of the old bulge epidermal structure provides a stable epidermal–neuronal interface and induces an lanceolate complex structure oriented toward the caudal side of the hair follicle.
source: Together these results indicate that the formation and preservation of the old bulge epidermal structure provides a stable epidermal–neuronal interface and induces an lanceolate complex structure oriented toward the caudal side of the hair follicle.
evidence: Conclusion based on hair cycle and plucking experiments

claim: Caudally polarized localization of Aδ-LTMRs underlies direction-selective responsiveness of Aδ-LTMRs to hair deflection.
source: Rutlin et al. (2014) reported that caudally polarized localization of Aδ-LTMRs underlies direction-selective responsiveness of Aδ-LTMRs to hair deflection
evidence: Supported by citation to Rutlin et al., 2014

claim: The unique tissue architecture generated by upper-bulge epidermal stem cells is involved in the directional selectivity of the lanceolate complexes.
source: Rutlin et al. (2014) reported that caudally polarized localization of Aδ-LTMRs underlies direction-selective responsiveness of Aδ-LTMRs to hair deflection, suggesting that the unique tissue architecture generated by upper-bulge epidermal stem cells is involved in the directional selectivity of the lanceolate complexes.
evidence: Inferred from connection between tissue architecture and functional properties

claim: Mid-bulge epidermal stem cells express many tendon-related genes and induce the differentiation of APMs and their correct anchorage to the bulge via secretion of the basement membrane protein nephronectin.
source: Our previous study also showed that the mid-bulge epidermal stem cells express many tendon-related genes and induce the differentiation of APMs and their correct anchorage to the bulge via secretion of the basement membrane protein nephronectin (Fujiwara et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujiwara et al., 2011

claim: Deletion of nephronectin moves the muscle near the upper-bulge.
source: Deletion of nephronectin moves the muscle near the upper-bulge.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge from previous work

claim: The morphology of the lanceolate complex was altered in the nephronectin mutant.
source: The morphology of the lanceolate complex was altered in the nephronectin mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G

claim: Heterogeneous epidermal stem cells are compartmentalized not only for efficient epidermal homeostasis and regeneration, but also for defining patterned niches for specific epidermal–dermal interactions, in part through providing different ECM environments.
source: Therefore, we propose that the heterogeneous epidermal stem cells are compartmentalized not only for efficient epidermal homeostasis and regeneration (Schepeler et al., 2014), but also for defining patterned niches for specific epidermal–dermal interactions, in part through providing different ECM environments.
evidence: Proposed based on findings from this study and citation to Schepeler et al., 2014

claim: The collar matrix has anatomical and functional features in common with the essential ECM in touch end organs of non-vertebrate organisms, such as the mantle in C. elegans.
source: The collar matrix has anatomical and functional features in common with the essential ECM in touch end organs of non-vertebrate organisms, such as the mantle in C. elegans (Emtage et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison based on literature citation to Emtage et al., 2004

claim: Electron-dense amorphous ECMs are likely to be the fundamental ECM regulating sensory end organ formation and function in multicellular organisms.
source: Thus, electron-dense amorphous ECMs are likely to be the fundamental ECM regulating sensory end organ formation and function in multicellular organisms.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on comparison with C. elegans

claim: Deletion of EGFL6 did not change the number or length of sensory axonal endings, electrical excitability of Aδ-LTMRs and gross skin histology.
source: Deletion of EGFL6 did not change the number or length of sensory axonal endings, electrical excitability of Aδ-LTMRs and gross skin histology.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from Egfl6 knockout analysis

claim: Defects in tactile responses in Egfl6 mutants were induced not by the loss or severe damage of touch sensory neurons themselves, but by the changes in the local ECM environment.
source: These results indicate that defects in tactile responses in the mutants were induced not by the loss or severe damage of touch sensory neurons themselves, but by the changes in the local ECM environment.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of defects observed in Egfl6 knockout mice

claim: The ECM can simultaneously function as both a tissue insulator and glue, keeping different cell populations and subcellular structures from intermingling.
source: The ECM can simultaneously function as both a tissue insulator and glue, keeping different cell populations and subcellular structures from intermingling.
evidence: General statement about ECM function based on established knowledge

claim: The ECM forms stable connections, or tethers, between sensory axon endings and their surroundings to transmit mechanical stimuli to axonal endings.
source: Moreover, it has been proposed that the ECM forms stable connections, or tethers, between sensory axon endings and their surroundings to transmit mechanical stimuli to axonal endings (Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zimmerman et al., 2014

claim: Integrins and integrin signalling genes are required for touch responses of touch receptor neurons in C. elegans.
source: Integrins and integrin signalling genes are required for touch responses of touch receptor neurons in C. elegans (Calixto et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calixto et al., 2010

claim: αv integrins accumulate at synapses of the central nervous system and play key roles in synapse development and function.
source: αv integrins accumulate at synapses of the central nervous system and play key roles in synapse development and function (Chavis and Westbrook, 2001; McCarty et al., 2005).
